messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 68

# Marcus

Marcus is a 63-year-old Māori construction worker who has spent most of his adult life building things with his hands — foundations, frameworks, structures meant to last. There is something quietly ironic in this, he admits, because for nearly eleven years the foundation of his own home was rotting from the inside.

His wife, Diane, was the kind of woman who could fill a room with warmth when she wanted to. She was also the kind of woman who, when the drinking started, could empty that same room of every safe feeling he had ever known. The physical violence began gradually — a shove during an argument, a thrown plate that caught his shoulder — and then accelerated into something he still struggles to name without lowering his voice. She broke two of his ribs during what would turn out to be the second-to-last year of their marriage. He told the foreman on his site that he'd taken a fall from scaffolding. Nobody questioned it. Men on construction sites fall.

Diane died of liver failure eight years ago. Marcus had not left her by then. He has spent considerable time trying to understand why, and the closest he can get is that leaving felt more dangerous than staying, and that somewhere along the way he had stopped believing he deserved better. When she died, he did not feel relief the way he had imagined he might. He felt something closer to freefall.

In the years since, Marcus has continued working — he is good at his job, respected on site, the kind of man younger workers go to when they need something done properly. But work has become one of the few places where he feels anything resembling competence. The noise and physicality of a construction site keep him anchored in the present in a way that the silence of his house does not. He lives alone now, and evenings are the worst of it. He sits with the television on but rarely watches it. What he is actually doing is listening — for footsteps, for a particular shift in the air, for the sound that used to precede the worst of it. His body has not yet learned that the threat is gone.

He sleeps poorly. When he does sleep, he often wakes from dreams that place him back in the kitchen of their old house, or in the hallway, or in the specific geometry of trying to make himself small in a space that offered nowhere to hide. He wakes with his heart hammering and sometimes does not know, for a few disorienting seconds, where or when he is. He has taken to sleeping with the light on.

Marcus does not talk about any of this with his workmates. The idea of it — of being known as a man who was beaten by his wife — produces a shame so acute it functions almost like a physical sensation, a tightening across his chest. He is aware, in some part of himself, that this shame is not entirely rational. He cannot talk himself out of it. He has become increasingly withdrawn from his adult children, cancelling plans, offering vague excuses, finding the effort of being present in a family setting overwhelming in ways he cannot explain to them.

He startles badly at raised voices. On site last month, two workers got into a heated argument near where he was working, and Marcus found himself walking away quickly, hands shaking, needing twenty minutes before he could return. He told himself he was getting a coffee.

What strikes him most, he says, is that he does not recognise himself. He was not always this way. He remembers a version of himself — younger, easier in his own skin, someone who laughed readily — and that person feels very far away now, like someone he used to know but has gradually lost touch with. He is not sure, sitting across from a therapist for the first time in his life, whether that man is still reachable. But he has come, and that, he says, is something.
